I used to ask every new dialysis patient the same thing: "What was your A1C before your kidneys failed?" After 11,000 patients and the same answer every single time, I stopped asking. It was always "managed." Always between 6.5 and 7.5. Always someone who'd been told to cut protein, reduce salt, and come back in six months. The chairs aren't full of people who ignored their kidneys. They're full of people who trusted the wrong number.

I'm telling you this now because last month I got my own prediabetes diagnosis with creeping creatinine — and I refuse to end up in one of my own chairs.

I'm a dialysis nurse. Fourteen years. Roughly 11,000 patients connected to machines. Let me tell you what that actually looks like.

The slow, irreversible slide. 10%. Then 20%. Then 50%. Until one day your doctor says: "You need dialysis. Three times a week. Four hours per session. For the rest of your life."

A needle goes into a fistula — a surgical access point in the arm that leaves a scar most patients hide under long sleeves even in summer.

The swelling in your legs, ankles, and face. Puffiness that makes you unrecognizable to your own grandchildren.

The dietary restrictions that make eating miserable. No potassium. No phosphorus. No salt. Bananas dangerous. Tomatoes dangerous. Cheese dangerous.

And the waiting list. Years. Sometimes a decade. Praying for a transplant that might never come.

I've watched marriages buckle under the schedule. I've watched grandchildren learn to plan around Grandma's dialysis days. I've watched a 61-year-old man read the same magazine in the waiting room every Tuesday and Thursday for three years while his wife was connected.

I've watched patients stop coming. I know what that means.

One of my long-term patients — Ruth, 63, three years in my unit — told me something I think about every day. She said: "This isn't living. This is just not dying yet."

Every. Single. One.

So here's the trap most people are stuck in. Two paths. Both lead to suffering.

Path one: Follow doctor's orders. Cut protein. Drink more water. Take the ACE inhibitor. Monitor labs every six months. Watch your kidney function drop year after year anyway.

Path two: Do nothing. Leave the damage unchecked. Foam in the toilet that won't go away. Ankles that swell by 4 PM. Crushing fatigue that won't lift no matter how much you rest.

Most people over the age of 50 tragically ignore these symptoms until it's too late. They blame the puffiness on age. They blame the fatigue on stress. They blame the foam on hard water.

It's none of those things. It's your kidneys screaming for help.

Last month I sat in my own doctor's office and heard "prediabetes" attached to my own name.

But I've heard those exact words from the charts of people now sitting in my chairs.

Here's what nobody explains to you.

Think of every cell in your body like a tiny room. On the walls there are doors — small protein doors called GLUT4 transporters. In a healthy body those doors stay open. Sugar comes through the blood, doors open, sugar goes inside, cell burns it for energy.

In an insulin-resistant body, those doors retreat. They pull away from the wall. The pancreas sends the signal — and they don't answer.

Then the tears get bigger. Then filtration drops. Then the system fails.

And it's not just kidneys.

That same sugar pileup strips the insulation off your nerves — that's why your feet burn. It starves your brain — that's why the fog rolls in by 2pm. ALL of it traces back to the same closed doors.

Your doctor monitors the headline number. The story underneath is your organs falling apart.

Now let me address what you're probably thinking.

First: "What about cutting protein?"

Cutting protein gives the torn mesh less to filter. It doesn't repair the mesh. It doesn't stop the sand. The tearing continues — quieter, but still happening.

Second: "I've been drinking more water."

Drinking more water flushes toxins. But it doesn't stop the friction tearing your filters. You're running more fluid through the same broken screens.

Third: "What about ACE inhibitors?"

ACE inhibitors slow the damage by reducing pressure. But the sand is still coming. The mesh is still tearing. Just slower.

All of these target pieces of the puzzle — but miss the complete mechanism. The doors are still closed. The sugar is still piling up. The damage continues underneath whatever you're doing on top.

The monitoring just measures how torn the mesh is getting. Nobody is stopping the sand.

Type-A Polymers and MHCP. Found in one specific plant — Ceylon cinnamon. Cinnamomum verum.

A 2003 study in Diabetes Care showed a 29% drop in fasting blood glucose. Research in Pharmacognosy Research mapped the GLUT4 mechanism — how these compounds bring those doors back to the surface.

And every time I bring this up with someone whose kidneys are declining, I get the look.

Wide eyes. Raised eyebrows.

That "You mean… cinnamon? The thing in my pumpkin pie? That's supposed to fix my kidneys?" face.

I get it. It sounds unrelated.

You can't patent a plant. No patent means no money. No sales reps, no training updates, no guideline changes.

Same hair. Same products. A different city. Suddenly, the routine can feel completely different.

Lucinn filters chlorine and heavy metals in the shower, giving the routine a more consistent, cleaner-water starting point wherever home is.

tr: After about a decade of doing hair, you start noticing patterns. And the biggest one nobody talks about is that I can usually guess what city a client moved from. Here are five things I've learned that I can't stop thinking about. Your scalp gets dehydrated way more than people realize, and here's the part that most people get wrong. When your scalp is dehydrated, it actually overproduces oil to compensate for it. So if your roots are greasy by midday, but your ends are dry and snapping off, that's because your scalp is dehydrated and it's overproducing oil to try and fix itself. And a huge part of what's causing that is the chlorine in your water, it strips your scalp every single time you wash. So then you wash it more because it's greasy, which strips it more, which makes it produce even more oil. That loop is what most people are trapped in, and they have no idea. Second thing, hard water messes with your hair way more than people realize, and it happens so slowly you don't even clock it. All those minerals build up on your scalp and on the hair shaft, and it basically blocks your products from absorbing properly. So you can be using the best shampoo, the best mask, doesn't matter, if the water's working against you the whole time. That's why I see people spending a fortune on products, and getting almost nothing out of them. Third thing, and this one actually surprised me. You'd think filtering your water would just fix all of this, but a lot of filters only strip stuff out, the chlorine, the heavy metals, all of it, and don't put anything back. So you end up with water that's technically cleaner, but kind of empty, and your skin can still feel stripped and dull after, because there's nothing left in the water to actually support it. Filtering isn't the same as filtering well. Fourth thing, your hair can physically change over time, depending on what you expose it to daily. Kind of like how your brain rewires itself with repetition, except this is your hair shaft. Repeated exposure to harsh, mineral-heavy water weakens the structure over time, more prone to snapping and breakage. But it goes both ways. Water that's actually good for your hair daily means your hair gets a chance to rebuild, instead of getting beat up every shower. This last one is going to be the most important thing I want you to take away today. Most people will chase every treatment, every bond builder, every 10-step routine, and never once think about the water touching their hair, every single time they wash it. It's not glamorous, nobody's talking about it, but it might genuinely be the most overlooked step in anyone's routine. This is why I have Lucene in my own shower, and why I tell clients to get one. It filters out the chlorine and heavy metals like I mentioned, but it also infuses nourishing minerals back into the water. So instead of stripped, dull water hitting your hair every day, you're actually getting something that supports it. Oh, and by the way, if you want to check out Lucene, I've left the link down below.
